Every key term, framework, and model in the program — what it means, where it comes from, and where it connects. This is the navigational layer that ties together learn/ → lessons/ → notes/canon/ → acumen/.

How to use: look up any concept. Read the definition, follow the source link for depth, check the applied-to examples for real-world use, and follow the "argues with" threads to see where other thinkers disagree. The disagreements are the compounding.

Financial Statements & Accounting

Revenue (top line) — Total money a company earns from its core business before any costs are subtracted. Source: Unit 01 · Applied: RCL, AAPL, PTON, DPZ, TXRH, NKE

Costs — Everything a company spends to generate revenue: materials, labor, rent, marketing, interest. Source: Unit 01 · Applied: RCL (fixed costs + COVID impact)

Profit / Net income (bottom line) — What's left after subtracting all costs from revenue. The accounting measure of whether a company made money. Source: Unit 01 · Applied: RCL, AAPL, NKE · Argues with: "Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact" → Unit 02

Net margin — Profit as a percentage of revenue (net income ÷ revenue × 100). How many cents of profit per dollar of sales. Source: Unit 01, Unit 04 · Applied: RCL, MA, AAPL

Income statement (P&L) — The financial report that shows revenue, costs, and profit over a period (quarter or year). A movie, not a photograph. Source: Unit 01 · Applied: RCL 2019/2020/2022

Cash flow statement — The financial report that tracks actual cash moving in and out of the business. Separates operating, investing, and financing flows. Source: Unit 02 · Applied: RCL

Operating cash flow (OCF) — Cash generated by the company's actual business operations, stripping out accounting adjustments. The "did customers actually pay us" number. Source: Unit 02 · Applied: RCL, AAPL (earnings quality check)

Depreciation — A non-cash accounting charge that spreads the cost of a big asset (ship, factory, building) over its useful life. Reduces reported profit but doesn't reduce cash. Source: Unit 02 · Applied: RCL (ships as non-cash charge)

Balance sheet — A snapshot of everything a company owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and the residual belonging to shareholders (equity) at one moment in time. A photograph, not a movie. Source: Unit 03 · Applied: RCL, AAPL

Assets — Everything a company owns or is owed: cash, buildings, inventory, accounts receivable, intellectual property. Source: Unit 03 · Applied: RCL, AAPL

Liabilities — Everything a company owes to others: loans, bonds, accounts payable, deferred revenue. Source: Unit 03 · Applied: RCL, AAPL

Equity — What's left for shareholders after subtracting liabilities from assets. The shock absorber — if assets drop, equity absorbs the blow before creditors lose anything. Source: Unit 03 · Applied: RCL, AAPL

Accounting equation (A = L + E) — Assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Every transaction must keep this equation balanced. Source: Unit 03 · Applied: AAPL 10-K note

Leverage (financial) — The ratio of liabilities to equity. Higher leverage means more borrowed money relative to owner money — more upside when things go well, more risk when they don't. Source: Unit 04 · Applied: RCL (capital-heavy business) · Disambiguate: one of three distinct meanings — financial (here), managerial (Grove, Leadership section), staff/pyramid (professional services leverage, Competitive Strategy section)

3-minute health check — A quick diagnostic combining three ratios: net margin (profitability), cash flow vs profit (earnings quality), and leverage (risk). Enough to form a first opinion on any public company. Source: Unit 04 · Applied: RCL capstone exercise

10-K — A company's annual report filed with the SEC. Contains audited financials, risk factors, management discussion, and business description. The single most important public document about any company. Source: Unit 01 · Applied: AAPL 10-K, NKE

Risk factors (Item 1A) — The section of a 10-K where a company lists everything that could go wrong. Changes year-over-year reveal what management is newly worried about. Source: Unit 08 · Applied: NKE (filing-language diff analysis)

MD&A (Management's Discussion and Analysis) — The section of a 10-K where management explains the numbers in their own words — what drove results, what they expect, what changed. Source: Unit 08

SEC / EDGAR — The Securities and Exchange Commission's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval system. Every public company's filings are freely available here. Source: Unit 01 · Applied: _ingest/edgar.py throughout the program

XBRL — eXtensible Business Reporting Language. A structured data format that tags every number in a filing so machines can read it. What makes edgar.py facts possible. Source: CURRICULUM.md · Applied: sec-filing-intelligence

Valuation & Investment

Growth (durable vs spike) — An increase in revenue or earnings over time. The critical distinction: durable growth (repeatable, compounding) vs spike growth (one-time surge that reverses). Source: Unit 05 · Applied: PTON boom/bust

Cash burn — The rate at which a company spends cash beyond what it earns. A company burning $50M/quarter with $200M in the bank has ~4 quarters of runway. Source: Unit 05 · Applied: PTON

Compounding — Growth on top of growth. A 1% daily improvement compounds to 37× in a year. The most powerful force in finance and learning. Source: Unit 05, Unit 10 · Applied: 1% rule in Atomic Habits

Present value — What a future cash flow is worth today, discounted for the time you have to wait and the risk you won't get it. A dollar tomorrow is worth less than a dollar today. Source: Unit 06 · Applied: PTON price collapse

Discounted cash flow (DCF) — A valuation method that estimates a company's worth by projecting its future cash flows and discounting them back to today's dollars. The conceptual foundation of all valuation. Source: Unit 06 · Applied: apply-stock-picking-nke

Market cap — The total value the stock market places on a company (share price × shares outstanding). What the crowd thinks the business is worth. Source: Unit 06

Capital expenditure (capex) — Money spent on long-lived assets: factories, equipment, ships, stores. The cost of staying in business for capital-heavy companies. Source: Unit 09 · Applied: DPZ vs TXRH

Capital-light / asset-light — A business model that generates revenue without owning expensive physical assets. Franchises, software, royalties. High margins, low reinvestment. Source: Unit 09 · Applied: DPZ (franchise model) · Contrast: Capital-heavy: RCL, TXRH

Royalty business — A model where you own the intellectual property or brand and collect a percentage of someone else's revenue for using it. Near-zero marginal cost. Source: Unit 09, media-practitioner · Applied: DPZ, Chick-fil-A, ARM · Via: Ackman thesis in Tiger Sisters

Margin of safety — The gap between what you pay and what you estimate something is worth. A buffer for being wrong. Buy a dollar for 65 cents, and you can be off by 35% and still not lose money. Source: Klarman · Applied: NKE stock pick, acumen case-01 · Argues with: Mauboussin — judge the process, not the outcome

Expectations investing — Reverse-engineering: start with the stock price, figure out what growth assumptions it implies, then ask whether those assumptions are reasonable. Source: Mauboussin · Applied: NKE stock pick

Khan's 7-step stock-picking — A structured process for evaluating a stock: understand the business, check the financials, assess the moat, value it, find the margin of safety, consider risks, then decide. Source: tiger-sisters-stock-picking · Applied: apply-stock-picking-nke

24/5 trading — U.S. equities trading continuously from Sunday 8pm to Friday 8pm ET. Only as "open" as its least-open layer: venue → tape (SIP) → clearing (NSCC 24x5, live June 2026) → settlement/funding (still 9-to-5) → humans. Equities converging on the structure Treasuries and FX already have. Source: 24/5 trading

Closing auction — The single 4pm ET match where index funds, mutual-fund NAVs, options settlement and VWAP benchmarks all coordinate. A Schelling focal point: extended hours haven't diluted it because everyone expects everyone else there. Source: 24/5 trading · Lens: Schelling

Adverse selection (in market making) — A market maker's core risk: the trader on the other side may know something. Thin sessions raise the ratio of informed to uninformed flow, so dealers widen spreads and cut depth — the "lemons premium" you pay to trade at 2am. Source: 24/5 trading · Lens: Akerlof

ETF premium / discount to NAV — The gap between an ETF's traded price and the value of its holdings. Normally arbitraged away by authorized participants; when the underlying market is closed (credit bonds overnight) it can't be, and the ETF price becomes the price discovery for the asset class. Source: 24/5 trading

Trade date roll — Under NSCC 24x5 the "trade date" changes at 8pm ET, not midnight: a 9pm Monday trade is a Tuesday trade for settlement, ex-dividend and record-date purposes. Source: 24/5 trading

Overnight Protected Hours — 9:00pm–4:00am ET, Sun–Thu. Under LULD Amendment No. 27 (SEC approved Aug 2026, effective Dec 6, 2026), trades and quotes outside ±20% bands are prevented. No automatic trading pause — but a discretionary Regulatory Halt does not reopen until the next session. A kill switch, not a circuit breaker. Source: 24/5 trading

Evaluated pricing — How illiquid bonds get marked when they haven't traded: a vendor model (BVAL, ICE) infers a price from comparable trades and quotes. Under 24/5 it starts ingesting overnight ETF prints — so a thin equity-session price becomes an input to the valuation of trillions in credit. Source: 24/5 trading · Tradeweb Ai-Price

TRACE — FINRA's tape for US corporate-bond trades. Dealers must report within 15 minutes (a reporting deadline, not a dissemination delay); each print carries a side flag (customer buy, customer sell, dealer-to-dealer), and sizes are capped on the public tape at "5MM+" for IG and "1MM+" for HY. The ground truth every bond-pricing model is scored against. Source: Tradeweb Ai-Price

Liquidity score — A vendor's rank of how easily a bond trades, built from depth, bid-offer, trade frequency and size. No common scale: Tradeweb 1–10, S&P 1–5, Bloomberg LQA and ICE 0–100. Accuracy claims bucketed by "liquidity score" are only comparable within one vendor. Source: Tradeweb Ai-Price

Last-print baseline — Scoring a pricing model against "the next trade will equal the last trade." The floor any model should beat. Unless the last print is matched to the same side (bid vs offer), the baseline absorbs bid/ask bounce and flatters the model. Source: Tradeweb Ai-Price · Lens: Tetlock (score against the right comparison class)

Reference price — The price the rest of the workflow keys off: auto-execution thresholds, RFQ evaluation, TCA, fund NAVs. Whoever supplies it collects recurring data revenue and switching costs. In credit: CP+ (MarketAxess, being acquired by ICE), Ai-Price (Tradeweb), BVAL, ICE, S&P (which licenses CP+). Source: Tradeweb Ai-Price · Lens: Shapiro & Varian

Overnight risk premium — The empirical finding that most of the historical US equity return accrued between the close and the next open rather than during the session. 24/5 makes it directly tradable — and therefore a candidate for arbitrage away. Source: 24/5 trading · Relevant to: quant-backtesting/

Business date as a first-class event — The 24/5 refactor pattern: replace the implicit "today" every post-trade system assumes with lifecycle events (session open/close, trade-date roll, clearing cutoff) emitted by one clock owner onto an ordered log, which every ledger, recon and report consumes. The diagnostic: grep the codebase for the business date. Source: 24/5 institutional response

Follow-the-sun — Operating model where regional teams hand off support across time zones with full context, so 2am ET is a shift, not an exception. Cboe's stated model for 24x5; OCC evaluating. The org half of the 24/5 problem. Source: 24/5 institutional response · Lens: Larson

Cell-based architecture — Partition a system into independent cells (by symbol range, account, region) so maintenance and failure affect one cell, not the whole. How you do change without a maintenance window. Pairs with canary-by-partition. Source: 24/5 institutional response

Market Institutions & Roles

Sell side — Raises capital for companies and sells securities to investors; advises on deals. Earns fees and commissions, so the incentive runs to volume. Investment banks and brokers. Entry-level roles are plentiful here. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §2 · Note: banks run buy-side arms too — "sell side" means the investment banking division specifically

Buy side — Invests other people's money. Earns a management fee regardless of outcome plus a performance fee, typically ~20% of gains. Asset managers, hedge funds, PE, VC, pension funds. Usually wants 2–4 years of experience first. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §2 · Applied: tiger sisters private capital 101

Front / middle / back office — The client-contact axis. Front (IB, S&T, research) faces clients and generates revenue; middle (risk, compliance, finance control) exists to constrain the front office; back (technology, operations) makes it run. A bank's org chart is substantially a risk-control artifact. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §2

Trader vs. salesperson — On a bank floor these are different jobs. The trader makes the price and owns the risk; the salesperson owns the client relationship. Pricing and relationship are deliberately separated. Traders are only 15–20% of a "trading floor." Source: trading-floor-mechanics §4

Flow trader — Executes large client orders by sourcing liquidity on both sides. Explicitly not an investor — a middleman earning commission and bid-ask spread. Distinct from a prop trader, who trades the firm's own capital. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §3

Agency vs. principal execution — In agency, the bank works your order into the market as your agent. In principal (the facilitation desk), the bank buys your line onto its own book and wears the risk — more expensive, but it gets size done now. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §4 · Relates to: 24/5 trading

Block trade — A single large transaction, threshold ~$10m or more than one day's average volume, negotiated privately rather than worked into the market. The market sees 5–10 small blocks a day; large ones come weekly to quarterly. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §4 · Applied: Auckland Airport $1.3bn sell-down

Wall crossing — Bringing a counterparty inside the information barrier by giving them material non-public information under restriction, so a block can be sourced privately. Routine in block trading, and the reason information barriers exist at all. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §4

Information barrier (Chinese wall) — Separation between parts of a firm that must not share information. Best implemented structurally rather than as policy: UBS uses carpet colour for physical zones and holds its 7:30 flow meeting and 7:45 research meeting separately so client flow cannot leak into research. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §4 · Lens: canon meadows thinking in systems — build the rule into the structure

Daily stop — A bounded, pre-set daily loss limit that also serves as the unit of account for discussing P&L ("I was up two daily stops, got out for half a daily stop"). Normalizes outcomes onto a comparable scale before they are ever debated. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §5

Accept the facts, refuse the judgment, build your own — The program's method, arrived at independently by three sources: a data architecture, an academic, and a working buy-side analyst. Take Layer 1 (reported facts) from any source; decline anyone else's derived conclusions; construct the drivers and assumptions yourself. Consult consensus after you have a number — before, it anchors you. Source: trading-floor-mechanics §3c · See spine 12 · Lens: canon kahneman thinking fast and slow

Research Instrumentation & Data Access

Bloomberg Terminal — The institutional financial data platform (~$25–30k/yr per seat). Command grammar is TICKER <asset key> FUNCTION <GO>; ~210 core function mnemonics. Its moat is not data — it is switching costs (muscle memory in the mnemonics) plus network economies (the IB messaging network the profession standardized on). Source: bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation · Argues with: sec-filing-intelligence on whether public filings equalize access

Information latency — The lag between a fact becoming true and a given observer being able to see it. Distinct from information access. A 13F discloses an institutional position up to 45 days after quarter-end; a block print is visible on a terminal in seconds. Same legal disclosure regime, ~7-week spread. Source: bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation §3 · Argues with: the "no information-asymmetry barrier" claim in sec-filing-intelligence — the corpus is symmetric; the clock is not · Why it matters: defines the boundary of what this program can instrument

Do-nothing counterfactual — The return from taking no action over the same window, computed before reading any strategy's result. A Bollinger strategy on MMM (2010–21) returned 133%; buy-and-hold returned 215% with dividends. Without the counterfactual, the interface presents an 82-point underperformance as a win. Source: bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation §5 · Applied: quant-backtesting/ · Argues with: nothing — it is the base rate canon mauboussin success equation demands and canon kahneman thinking fast and slow WYSIATI suppresses

Consensus estimates — The aggregated forecast of sell-side analysts for a company's future revenue and earnings. The number a company "beats" or "misses." Not in EDGAR — filings are historical, estimates are forward. Source: bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation §2 · Terminal: EEO ANR EE

Short interest — The percentage of a company's freely-tradeable shares (float) that have been sold short. A crowding and sentiment measure. FINRA publishes biweekly and lagged; terminals show it live. Source: bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation §2 · Terminal: SI SIA

Supply-chain graph — A mapped network of a company's suppliers and customers with the revenue and cost exposure attached to each. Reveals concentration risk before it appears in results. Reconstructable from 10-K major-customer disclosure, one company at a time, expensively. Source: bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation · Terminal: SPLC · Relates to: Unit 07 moats, customer concentration as a moat inverse

Constraint audit — Asking of any analytical call: did this depend on data the analyst could not have obtained, and was the dependency acknowledged? A call resting silently on unobtainable data is not uncertain — it is unfounded, and should score differently. Source: bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation §6 · Applied: proposed red-team input for acumen/MECHANISM.md

Competitive Strategy & Moats

Competitive advantage / Moat — Something that lets a company earn above-normal profits for a sustained period because competitors can't easily copy it. Source: Unit 07 · Applied: MA vs RCL · Argues with: Porter ↔ Helmer ↔ Christensen — three different frameworks for what moats are and how they work

Network effect — A product or service that becomes more valuable as more people use it. Each new user makes the existing users' experience better. Source: Unit 07, Parker · Applied: 24/5 trading, Crexi, Snap

Commodity business — An industry where the product is interchangeable and the customer buys on price alone. No pricing power, thin margins, brutal competition. Source: Unit 07 · Applied: Cruise lines

Five Forces — Porter's framework for analyzing industry profitability: threat of new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes, and intensity of rivalry. Source: Porter · Applied: core-04 lesson, JPM report · Argues with: Helmer — if you can't name the barrier, you don't have a moat

7 Powers — Helmer's taxonomy of durable competitive advantages: scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource, and process power. Each requires both a benefit and a barrier. Source: Helmer · Applied: JPM defensibility matrix, DRAMA crossref, acumen case-01 · Argues with: Porter — forces describe the battlefield; powers explain why you win

Counter-positioning — Adopting a business model that an incumbent can't copy without damaging its existing business. The classic disruptor advantage. Source: Helmer · Applied: Netflix vs Blockbuster

Disruptive innovation — When a cheaper, simpler product starts at the bottom of a market and gradually moves upmarket until it displaces the incumbent. The incumbent ignores it because it doesn't serve their best customers — until it does. Source: Christensen · Applied: 24/5 trading, JPM AI disruption analysis · Argues with: Porter/Helmer — not every new entrant disrupts

Value stick (WTP / WTS) — A company creates value by raising customers' willingness-to-pay (WTP) or lowering suppliers' willingness-to-sell (WTS). Profit is the firm's share of the gap. Source: core-04 lesson · Applied: Netflix vs Disney

Co-opetition / Value Net — Brandenburger & Nalebuff's framework: business is not purely competitive — competitors are also complementors who expand the pie. Map the full value net before choosing moves. Source: Brandenburger & Nalebuff · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Porter's zero-sum framing

PARTS — Brandenburger & Nalebuff's five levers for changing the game: Players, Added value, Rules, Tactics, Scope. Source: Brandenburger & Nalebuff · Gap: never applied

Platform envelopment — When a platform in one market leverages its user base and data to enter and dominate an adjacent market. Source: Cusumano, Parker · Applied: Amazon Basics, Apple "Sherlocking"

Staff leverage (professional-services leverage) — The ratio of fee-earners below an equity partner to equity partners. The partner originates and supervises; associates execute; the firm bills their hours at a multiple of what it pays for them. Revenue scales with headcount under the partner, not with partner effort. The operating model of law, consulting, accounting, and agencies. Source: professional-services leverage · Applied: Kirkland & Ellis (~5–6:1, $10.56B rev) vs. Wachtell Lipton (~2.4:1) · Argues with: Grove — staff leverage multiplies billings (margin capture), managerial leverage multiplies output (value creation); not the same claim

Cravath system — Paul Cravath's early-20th-century template for the tiered firm: recruit a large class from brand-name schools into codified training, promote only a select few to partnership. Structurally a tournament — the deferred prize buys 2,000+ billable hours a year at a fraction of the realized bill rate. It is what produces the pyramid; the pyramid is not an accident of growth. Source: professional-services leverage · Breaks when: promotion odds visibly collapse, or growth flattens and the base stops widening

Billable hour — Pricing by units of expert time. The complement to staff leverage: leverage supplies the bodies, the hour is the meter that converts bodies into revenue. Because comp is fixed, each fee-earner has a breakeven hour count past which marginal hours are near-pure profit — and below which they are near-pure loss. Source: professional-services leverage · Argues with: fixed/outcome pricing — an attack on the pricing unit is an attack on the leverage model itself (the AI thesis)

Profits per equity partner (PPP) — A partnership's profit pool ÷ equity partners. The Big Law scoreboard, and a ratio with a small denominator: it measures how good a seat is, not how large or durable the franchise is. Wachtell's >$12M beats Kirkland's ~$11M while Kirkland's absolute profit pool is roughly an order of magnitude larger. The same error as judging a company by EPS while ignoring share count. Source: professional-services leverage · Applied: Kirkland vs. Wachtell 2025

Strategy & Decision-Making

Strategy kernel — Rumelt's three-part structure of good strategy: (1) a diagnosis of the challenge, (2) a guiding policy for dealing with it, and (3) coherent actions that carry out the policy. Source: Rumelt · Applied: acumen case-01 · Argues with: Lafley — five-choice cascade instead of a kernel

The Crux — The single most important challenge that is also solvable. The hard part of the problem that, if you crack it, unlocks everything else. Strategy is concentrating resources against the crux. Source: Rumelt · Applied: acumen case-01, DRAMA crossref · Argues with: Goldratt — the bottleneck, not the crux

Playing to Win (5 choices) — Lafley & Martin's strategy cascade: (1) winning aspiration, (2) where to play, (3) how to win, (4) required capabilities, (5) management systems. Each must nest inside the one above. Source: Lafley & Martin · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Rumelt — problem-first kernel vs aspiration-first cascade

Mission command (Auftragstaktik) — Tell people what to achieve and why, then let them figure out how. Push authority to where the information lives. Source: Bungay · Applied: media-practitioner (Commander's Intent)

Knowledge / Alignment / Effects gaps — Bungay's three gaps between plan and reality: (1) you don't know enough, (2) people don't understand the plan the same way, (3) actions don't produce the intended results. Source: Bungay · Gap: never applied

Day 1 vs Day 2 — Bezos's distinction: Day 1 is building with urgency, speed, customer obsession. Day 2 is stasis, irrelevance, decline. The goal is to always stay in Day 1. Source: Bezos · Applied: operator playbook, Tiger Sisters

Two-way door / One-way door — Bezos's decision taxonomy: reversible decisions (two-way doors) should be made fast by individuals; irreversible decisions (one-way doors) deserve careful deliberation. Source: Bezos · Applied: 24/5 institutional response, operator playbook, acumen case-01

Reversibility as a durability axis (labor-economics extension of the above) — A role's durability equals the share of its value sitting at a one-way door: an irreversible, accountable, high-magnitude act. Reversible work (drafts, research, review — anything a second pass can undo) gets absorbed by AI; irreversible accountability does not. Sorts jobs better than "routine vs. creative," since much creative work is reversible and much dull work (the attestation) is not. Roles split rather than vanish — the reversible half is absorbed, the remainder concentrates at the gate. Source: professional-services leverage §6 (own framework) · Applied: junior associates (heavy compression) vs. partners (durable, fewer seats) · Extends: Bezos — same axis, but the dependent variable is job durability, not decision speed

Accountability wall (licensure as moat) — Where law requires a licensed human to be accountable for an irreversible act — the lawyer's signature, the CPA's attestation, the PE's stamp, the fiduciary's liability — agents cannot cross by capability, only by deregulation. Licensure stops being merely a barrier to entry and becomes the wall around the one-way door. This is the floor under professional-services leverage compression: the pyramid thins toward a credentialed apex rather than disappearing. Source: professional-services leverage §6b · Applied: Harvey disclaims output accuracy; the partner's signature remains the liable act

Apprenticeship collapse — The reversible tasks AI absorbs are the entry rungs, which are simultaneously the automatable tier and the training pipeline to the durable senior apex. The pipeline from entry rung to door-owner is itself a one-way door — a broken skill ladder rebuilds slowly and with fidelity loss. The pyramid's unpriced second product is partners; automating the base optimizes revenue while destroying the succession function. Source: professional-services leverage §6d · Evidence: hiring of 22–25-year-olds into exposed roles down ~14% while senior roles hold · Argues with: Goldratt — optimizing a local metric against system throughput

Disagree and commit — When a team can't reach consensus, the leader picks a direction and everyone commits fully — even those who disagreed. Prevents both paralysis and passive sabotage. Source: Bezos · Applied: operator playbook

OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) — A goal-setting system: an Objective says what you want to achieve (qualitative, inspiring); Key Results say how you'll know you got there (quantitative, specific). Hitting 100% means you sandbagged; 70% is the sweet spot. Source: Doerr, Grove · Applied: Tiger Sisters · Argues with: 4DX — WIGs (Wildly Important Goals) compete with the same attention

Strategic inflection point — The moment when a 10× force (technology, regulation, customer shift) breaks your existing strategy. Senior people are usually the last to see it because they're most invested in the current model. Source: Grove · Applied: acumen case-01 (Intel)

Negotiation & Influence

BATNA (Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement) — Your walk-away option. Your power in any negotiation equals how good your BATNA is. Always know yours; try to learn theirs. Source: Fisher & Ury · Applied: Tiger Sisters (salary negotiation scripts) · Argues with: Voss — empathy and emotion drive outcomes more than frameworks

ZOPA (Zone of Possible Agreement) — The overlap between both sides' worst acceptable deals. If your ZOPA exists, a deal is possible; if it doesn't, walk away. Source: Fisher & Ury

Integrative negotiation — Expanding the pie before dividing it. Most negotiations have compatible interests hiding behind incompatible positions — find them by asking why, not arguing about what. Source: Fisher & Ury · Applied: Tiger Sisters ("the orange" example)

Tactical empathy — Voss's approach: name the other person's emotion out loud ("It seems like you're frustrated about…"). Labeling a negative emotion shrinks it; labeling a positive one reinforces it. Source: Voss · Applied: Tiger Sisters · Argues with: Fisher & Ury — principled/interests-based approach

Mirroring — Repeating the last 1-3 words someone said. They'll elaborate, revealing information they wouldn't have volunteered. Source: Voss · Applied: Tiger Sisters

Six principles of persuasion — Cialdini's toolkit: reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, and scarcity. The levers that move people whether they're aware of it or not. Source: Cialdini · Applied: Tiger Sisters ("because" effect) · Argues with: Carnegie — sincerity over mechanism

Pre-suasion — What you do before making a request shapes how it's received. Prime the audience's attention toward concepts that make your message more persuasive. Source: Cialdini · Applied: Tiger Sisters (back-channel prep)

SBI feedback (Situation-Behavior-Impact) — A feedback structure: describe the Situation, the specific Behavior you observed, and its Impact. Separates observation from judgment. Source: Tiger Sisters / Scott · Applied: Tiger Sisters (worked scripts)

Pyramid Principle (MECE) — Minto's communication structure: answer first, then support. Every supporting argument must be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE). The audience gets the conclusion up front. Source: Minto · Applied: Tiger Sisters (SCQA), acumen memo format · Argues with: Duarte — story-first, not answer-first

SCQA (Situation-Complication-Question-Answer) — An opener framework: establish the Situation (what everyone agrees on), introduce the Complication (what changed), pose the Question (what we need to solve), deliver the Answer (your recommendation). Source: Tiger Sisters · Applied: Tiger Sisters (worked examples)

Behavioral & Decision Science

System 1 / System 2 — Kahneman's two modes of thinking: System 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive, and effortless (but error-prone); System 2 is slow, deliberate, analytical, and effortful (but lazy). Source: Kahneman · Applied: tiger-sisters-stock-picking · Argues with: Klein — expert intuition is System 1, and it works in regular environments

Anchoring — Judgment pulled toward the first number you see, even if it's irrelevant. A random "65" on a spinner makes people guess higher on unrelated questions. Source: Kahneman · Applied: Tiger Sisters (salary negotiation)

Loss aversion — Losing $100 hurts roughly twice as much as gaining $100 feels good. People will take irrational risks to avoid losses. Source: Kahneman, Ariely

Nudge / Choice architecture — People's decisions are shaped by how options are presented. Defaults are the most powerful nudge — most people stick with whatever is pre-selected. Source: Thaler & Sunstein · Gap: never applied

Recognition-primed decisions (RPD) — Klein's model of how experts actually decide: they pattern-match from experience, mentally simulate one option, and execute if it works — they don't compare alternatives. Trust this in regular environments with repeated feedback. Source: Klein · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Kahneman — expert intuition is dangerous in irregular environments

Noise — Random scatter in judgments that should be consistent. Two judges see the same case and give wildly different sentences. Unlike bias (systematic error), noise is invisible until you measure it. Source: Kahneman, Sibony & Sunstein · Gap: never applied

Superforecasting — Tetlock's finding: a measurable minority of people forecast consistently better than experts and algorithms. What they do is learnable — think in probabilities, update incrementally, seek disconfirming evidence, keep score. Source: Tetlock · Applied: tiger-sisters-stock-picking

Latticework of mental models — Munger's prescription: you need models from many disciplines (psychology, physics, biology, economics, math) applied in combination. A single model is a hammer; every problem looks like a nail. Source: Munger · Applied: tiger-sisters-stock-picking

Inversion — Instead of asking "how do I succeed?", ask "how would I guarantee failure?" then avoid that. Clarifies thinking by flipping the question. Source: Munger · Applied: Tiger Sisters, acumen red-team

Skill vs luck — Mauboussin's continuum: most outcomes mix skill and luck, but we systematically over-attribute to skill. The more skill converges across competitors, the more luck determines who wins (the paradox of skill). Source: Mauboussin · Applied: Multiple practitioner notes

Leadership & Organizations

Managerial leverage — A manager's output = the output of their team + the output of teams they influence. Some activities (1-on-1s, training, setting direction) produce far more output per unit of time than others. Source: Grove · Applied: media-practitioner (meetings as leverage) · Argues with: staff leverage (professional services leverage) — Grove multiplies output and needs no one under-compensated; the pyramid multiplies billings on a spread

Task-Relevant Maturity (TRM) — Calibrate your management style to the person's experience with that specific task, not their seniority. Low TRM: be directive. High TRM: delegate and monitor. Source: Grove · Applied: media-practitioner

Radical Candor — The intersection of caring personally and challenging directly. Most people default to Ruinous Empathy (caring but not challenging) — being nice instead of being honest. Source: Scott · Applied: Tiger Sisters (SBI scripts) · Argues with: Carnegie — never criticize directly

Execution (3 core processes) — Bossidy & Charan's thesis: execution is a discipline, not a detail. The three core processes — people, strategy, and operations — must be linked tightly. Source: Bossidy & Charan · Gap: never applied

Culture = what you do under pressure — Horowitz's definition: culture is not your stated values; it's the pattern of behavior that gets rewarded, especially in hard cases. Who you promote and fire are the loudest cultural signals. Source: Horowitz · Applied: media-practitioner · Argues with: Schein — diagnose the invisible assumptions, not just the visible behavior

Org culture layers — Schein's three levels: (1) Artifacts (visible: office, rituals, language), (2) Espoused values (what people say they believe), (3) Basic underlying assumptions (what they actually believe, unconsciously). The dysfunction lives in the gap between 2 and 3. Source: Schein · Applied: media-practitioner · Argues with: Horowitz — engineer the behavior; the assumptions follow

8 steps of change — Kotter's sequence: (1) create urgency, (2) build a guiding coalition, (3) form a vision, (4) communicate it, (5) remove barriers, (6) generate short-term wins, (7) don't let up, (8) anchor in culture. Most fail at step 1 (insufficient urgency) or step 7 (declaring victory too early). Source: Kotter · Applied: media-practitioner · Argues with: Heath (Switch) — Rider/Elephant/Path works bottom-up, not top-down

Rider / Elephant / Path — Heath & Heath's change model: the Rider (rational mind) provides direction, the Elephant (emotional mind) provides energy, the Path (environment) makes the right behavior easy. Most change efforts coach the Rider and ignore the Elephant. Source: Heath & Heath · Applied: Tiger Sisters · Argues with: Kotter — 8 steps work top-down; Switch works bottom-up

Intent-based leadership — Marquet's model: replace "leader-follower" with "leader-leader." The language shift: "I intend to…" instead of "Permission to…" Two preconditions: competence (they know enough) and clarity (they understand the purpose). Source: Marquet · Applied: media-practitioner

Theory of constraints (TOC) — Goldratt's principle: every system has one constraint (bottleneck) that limits total throughput. Optimizing anything that isn't the bottleneck is an illusion of progress. Five steps: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat. Source: Goldratt · Applied: 24/5 trading · Argues with: Meadows — systems have multiple leverage points, not one constraint

Lean / Toyota Production System — Ohno's system: relentlessly eliminate waste (muda), build quality into the process (jidoka / "stop the line"), and produce only what's needed when it's needed (just-in-time). The seven wastes: overproduction, waiting, transport, overprocessing, inventory, motion, defects. Source: Ohno · Applied: 24/5 institutional response

Agency theory — Jensen & Meckling: whenever an agent acts on behalf of a principal, their interests diverge. The gap is the agency cost. Three solutions: monitoring, bonding (skin in the game), and incentive alignment. Source: Jensen & Meckling · Applied: EYL, Harlem Capital (GP/LP), Tiger Sisters

Team production / Shirking — Alchian & Demsetz: when output depends on a team, individual contribution is hard to measure, so people shirk. The firm exists to solve this — the residual claimant (owner) monitors to keep the team productive. Source: Alchian & Demsetz · Applied: operator playbook

Four team states — Larson's diagnostic: every team is in one of four states — falling behind, treading water, repaying debt, or innovating. You cannot fix a falling-behind team by adding goals; you fix it by adding people or cutting scope. Source: Larson · Applied: 24/5 institutional response, media-practitioner

Mechanism — Not a process or a policy: a complete loop with three legs — a tool, driven adoption of the tool, and inspection of the results, feeding course corrections. It takes controllable inputs and turns them into ongoing outputs on a recurring problem. Drop any leg and you have a good intention: tool without adoption = shelfware; tool + adoption without inspection = theatre. Source: AWS — Building Mechanisms & the ORR, Bezos · Applied: learn/VALIDATION.md (all three legs), acumen/MECHANISM.md (rebuilt after the legs were missing) · Argues with: Doerr — OKRs set direction but carry no adoption or inspection leg; the mechanism is what makes an OKR actually happen

Mechanism vs. guardrail — A guardrail is a wall that engages only in an emergency; a mechanism is a slope that re-centres you continuously. The image is a train wheel: the flange touches the rail only in a crisis, while the sloped tread re-centres the train on every rotation. Design the slope, not the wall. Source: AWS — Building Mechanisms · Argues with: Thaler & Sunstein — the same insight from behavioural economics: a default beats a mandate

Input metric vs. output metric — An output metric is the scoreboard (revenue, customers, margin): lagging, and if it falls it doesn't tell you what to do. An input metric is one you can change through your own actions this week and that shows up in the customer's experience. Two tests for a good input: controllable and customer-facing. A third, negative test: if it can be moved by manipulating it rather than by doing the work, it will be. Source: AWS — Building Mechanisms & the ORR · Applied: acumen/JUDGMENT-LEDGER.md (reps/week, unprompted crux rate, calibration error — replacing corpus-size counts) · Argues with: Walsh — "the standard of performance is the input; the score is a lagging byproduct"; 4DX calls the same thing a lead measure

Meta-inspection (correction of error) — The question that audits the mechanism rather than the work: would this mechanism have prevented the last failure? AWS's incident template asks "would any ORR recommendations have reduced or avoided the impact of this event?", so every failure grades the thing meant to prevent it. Without it, a mechanism's compliance rate gets reported while the outcome it exists to move never does. Source: AWS — Building Mechanisms & the ORR · Applied: acumen/MECHANISM.md — "which canon note, had I read it, would have changed this memo?" · Argues with: Bezos — "the process can become the thing"; this is the only defence in the material

Incentive compatibility — A mechanism is incentive-compatible when telling the truth is each party's best strategy regardless of what anyone else does. The practical test: if a mechanism runs on numbers self-reported by the people those numbers judge, it rewards misreporting. Its companion is information privacy — you rarely need the private information, only the party's response to a proposal, so iterate offers instead of demanding disclosure. Source: AWS — Building Mechanisms & the ORR (Amazon Science, VCG + Consensus Planning Protocol) · Argues with: Jensen & Meckling — agency theory solves divergence by monitoring; incentive compatibility removes the need to monitor by making honesty dominant

Value mapping — Turning an outcome you owe into a controllable input you can move, explicitly enough to be proven wrong. One row: outcome → output metric → measured baseline with a date → controllable input → expected direction and size of effect → owner → instrumentation → mechanism → inspection cadence. An empty cell is the work; an unfillable instrumentation cell means you cannot tell whether the bet paid off. Source: AWS — Building Mechanisms & the ORR · Argues with: Rumelt — the map is worthless without a diagnosis; naming inputs is not a substitute for naming the crux

Game Theory

Nash equilibrium — A state where no player can improve their outcome by changing their strategy alone. Everyone is doing the best they can given what everyone else is doing. Source: Dixit & Nalebuff · Applied: canon-game-theory lesson

Backward induction — Solve a sequential game by starting at the end and working backward. At each step, ask: "Knowing what comes next, what would a rational player do here?" Source: Dixit & Nalebuff · Gap: never applied

Tit for Tat — Axelrod's finding: in repeated interactions, the winning strategy is simple — cooperate first, then mirror whatever the other player did last. Nice, retaliatory, forgiving, and clear. Source: Axelrod · Applied: canon-game-theory lesson

Focal points (Schelling points) — When people can't communicate, they converge on the solution that seems "obvious" or "natural." Coordination without communication — meet at Grand Central, noon, at the clock. Source: Schelling · Applied: 24/5 trading

Credible commitment — Making your threat or promise believable by visibly limiting your own options. Burning the bridge behind you proves you won't retreat. Source: Schelling · Gap: never applied

Complementors — Players whose products or services make yours more valuable (and vice versa). Intel and Microsoft were complementors — better chips sold more copies of Windows. Source: Brandenburger & Nalebuff · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Porter — Five Forces has no role for complementors

Systems Thinking

Leverage points — Meadows's 12 places to intervene in a system, ranked from least to most powerful. Most people push at the bottom (tweaking numbers); the highest leverage is changing the system's goals or paradigm. Source: Meadows · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Goldratt — one constraint vs 12 leverage points

Stocks & flows / Feedback loops — Stocks are accumulations (water in a bathtub); flows are rates of change (faucet and drain). Reinforcing loops amplify; balancing loops stabilize. Most org problems are structural — replace the person but keep the structure, and you get the same behavior. Source: Meadows · Gap: never applied

Systems archetypes — Senge's recurring structural patterns: "shifting the burden" (quick fix atrophies the real solution), "limits to growth" (success hits a constraint), "tragedy of the commons" (shared resources overused). Source: Senge · Gap: never applied

The bullwhip effect — Small changes in consumer demand amplify into wild swings as you move upstream in a supply chain. Each link over-reacts to the signal from the link below it. Source: Sterman · Gap: never applied

Normal accidents — Perrow's thesis: in systems that are both tightly coupled and interactively complex, serious accidents aren't anomalies — they're inevitable ("normal"). You can't engineer them away; you can only choose to reduce coupling or reduce complexity. Source: Perrow · Applied: 24/5 trading

Black Swan — A rare event with three properties: (1) it's an outlier beyond normal expectations, (2) it has extreme impact, (3) after the fact, people construct explanations that make it seem predictable. We systematically blind ourselves to them. Source: Taleb · Applied: tiger-sisters-stock-picking · Argues with: Tetlock — forecasting is learnable, even in fat-tailed domains

Antifragile / Barbell strategy — Beyond robust: antifragile systems gain from stress and disorder. The barbell strategy: combine extreme safety (90% in boring, protected assets) with small, capped-downside, high-upside bets (10%). Source: Taleb · Applied: 24/5 trading, tiger-sisters-wealth-mechanics

Friction / Fog of war — Clausewitz's observation: in execution, everything is harder than it looks. Plans break on contact with reality because of incomplete information (fog), resistance (friction), and chance. Source: Clausewitz · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Bungay — adapted Clausewitz's military concepts for business organizations

Culminating point — The point past which further advance becomes self-destructive. The army that overextends its supply lines; the company that expands past its competence. Source: Clausewitz · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Thucydides — the Sicilian Expedition as the canonical overreach

Entrepreneurship & Venture

Lean Startup / MVP — Ries's method: a startup is a search vehicle under extreme uncertainty. Build the smallest thing that tests your riskiest assumption (MVP), measure whether it works (validated learning), then pivot or persevere. Source: Ries · Applied: operator playbook (Concierge MVP) · Argues with: Thiel — bold, non-incremental bets over iterative search

Zero to One — Thiel's thesis: creating something genuinely new (0→1) is categorically different from copying what works (1→n). Competition is overrated; the goal is monopoly built on real differentiation. Source: Thiel · Applied: Harlem Capital, Tiger Sisters · Argues with: Ries — iterate vs commit to a bold bet

Product discovery / 4 risks — Cagan's framework: before building anything, assess four risks: value (will anyone want it?), usability (can they use it?), feasibility (can we build it?), and viability (does it work for the business?). Source: Cagan · Applied: operator playbook

Sean Ellis test — Ask users "How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?" If fewer than 40% say "very disappointed," you haven't found product-market fit yet. Source: operator playbook · Applied: Segment, Vanta

LTV:CAC — Lifetime Value to Customer Acquisition Cost ratio. How much a customer is worth over their lifetime divided by how much it cost to acquire them. Below 3:1 is usually unsustainable. Source: operator playbook · Applied: Uber (-$0.22/ride)

LBO (Leveraged Buyout) — Buying a company using mostly borrowed money, using the company's own cash flows to repay the debt. The buyer puts up little equity; the upside is amplified but so is the risk. Source: tiger-sisters-private-capital · Applied: Toys "R" Us (failed LBO), Hilton (successful — Blackstone)

GP/LP / Carry / J-curve — Fund structure: General Partners (GPs) manage the fund and make investments; Limited Partners (LPs) provide the capital. Carry is the GP's share of profits (typically 20%). The J-curve: returns are negative early (fees + losses) before turning positive. Source: Harlem Capital · Applied: Harlem Capital fund economics · Argues with: Agency theory (Jensen-Meckling) — GP/LP is a principal-agent problem

Platform cold-start — The chicken-and-egg problem: a platform needs both sides to be valuable, but neither side joins without the other. Solutions: seed one side, offer single-player utility first, recruit marquee users. Source: Parker, Cusumano · Applied: operator playbook

Personal Effectiveness

Quadrant 2 — Covey's time-management matrix: important but not urgent tasks (exercise, learning, relationship-building, planning). Most people spend their time in Quadrant 1 (urgent + important) and Quadrant 3 (urgent + unimportant), starving Q2. Source: Covey · Applied: Tiger Sisters (calendar alignment)

Deep work — Newport's thesis: the ability to focus without distraction on a cognitively demanding task is simultaneously rare and valuable. Protect uninterrupted blocks; most people max out at ~4 hours/day. Source: Newport · Applied: Tiger Sisters (essentialism)

Habit loop / 4 laws — Clear's system for building habits: (1) make it obvious (cue), (2) make it attractive (craving), (3) make it easy (response), (4) make it satisfying (reward). Identity-based: "I am the type of person who…" Source: Clear · Applied: Tiger Sisters (identity-based habits) · Argues with: Covey — character-based vs system-based change

2-minute rule — If a new habit takes less than two minutes, you'll actually do it. Scale down any habit until the gateway version is trivially small, then build from there. Source: Clear

Personal Finance (Unit 10)

Index fund — A fund that buys every stock in a market index (like the S&P 500) instead of trying to pick winners. Low fees, broad diversification, historically beats most active managers. Source: Unit 10

401k match — Free money from your employer: they match your retirement contributions up to a percentage. Not contributing enough to get the full match is leaving compensation on the table. Source: Unit 10

Emergency fund — 3-6 months of expenses in cash (or near-cash) so a job loss, medical bill, or car repair doesn't force you into debt. The foundation before any investing. Source: Unit 10

4% safe withdrawal rate — A rule of thumb: if you withdraw 4% of your portfolio in year one and adjust for inflation each year after, historically the money lasts 30+ years. Source: Unit 10

30× income target — A rough financial independence benchmark: accumulate ~30× your annual expenses, which at a 3-4% withdrawal rate replaces your income indefinitely. Source: Unit 10

5-layer personal finance OS — The Unit 10 architecture: (1) earn, (2) protect (emergency fund + insurance), (3) eliminate debt, (4) invest (401k → IRA → taxable), (5) optimize (tax strategies, Mega Backdoor Roth, real estate). Source: Unit 10

Mega Backdoor Roth — A strategy to contribute up to ~$69k/year to a Roth account by making after-tax 401k contributions and converting them. Only works if your employer's plan allows it. Source: Unit 10

HYSA / MMF / CDs / Treasuries — Cash-equivalent instruments for emergency funds and short-term savings. HYSAs (High-Yield Savings Accounts) and MMFs (Money Market Funds) are liquid; CDs (Certificates of Deposit) and Treasuries lock up money for slightly higher yields. Source: Unit 10

Family office of one — Running your personal finances with the discipline of a family office: consolidated view, quarterly review cadence, asset allocation policy, tax optimization, estate basics. Source: Unit 10, Tiger Sisters

Communication & Storytelling

Resonate (what is / what could be) — Duarte's presentation structure: alternate between current reality ("what is") and proposed future ("what could be"). The gap between them creates tension that pulls the audience forward. End on "the new bliss" — the future realized. Source: Duarte · Applied: operator playbook · Argues with: Minto — logic first, not story first

Golden Circle (Start with Why) — Sinek's framework: communicate from the inside out — Why (purpose/belief) → How (process) → What (product). People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. Source: Sinek · Applied: operator playbook

Data-ink ratio — Tufte's principle: in a data visualization, every mark should encode data, not decoration. Minimize "chartjunk" (gratuitous gridlines, 3-D effects, gradients). Let the data speak. Source: Tufte · Gap: never applied

Ethics & History

Right vs right — Badaracco's framing: the hardest ethical decisions aren't right vs wrong — they're right vs right. Two legitimate values in conflict (loyalty vs truth, individual vs community). Source: Badaracco · Gap: never applied · Argues with: Sandel — three competing lenses of justice

Three lenses of justice — Sandel's three approaches: (1) maximize welfare (utilitarianism), (2) respect freedom (libertarian/Kantian rights), (3) cultivate virtue (Aristotelian). Each is powerful; each has a blind spot. Source: Sandel · Gap: never applied

Three models of decision — Allison's thesis (from the Cuban Missile Crisis): decisions can be explained through three different lenses: (1) rational actor, (2) organizational process, (3) governmental/bureaucratic politics. Most people default to lens 1 and miss 2 and 3. Source: Allison · Gap: never applied

Known / Unclear / Presumed — Neustadt & May's decision tool: separate what you know from what's unclear from what you're presuming. Most bad historical analogies fail because presumptions are treated as facts. Source: Neustadt & May · Gap: never applied

Thucydides Trap — When a rising power threatens an established power, structural fear makes conflict likely (though not inevitable). The pattern from the Peloponnesian War applied to modern geopolitics. Source: Thucydides · Gap: never applied

Capital Markets, Credit & Rates (Wall Street Skinny batch)

Enterprise value (EV) — What it costs to buy the whole business: equity value plus net debt. The price of the operations regardless of how they are financed; equity value is just the slice belonging to shareholders. Source: wss capital markets ma, wss technicals career · Applied: X/xAI ($33B equity + $12B debt) · Argues with: equity-value-only multiples in Unit 06

Equity check — The share of a buyout funded with the buyer's own money. Sets who takes the first loss; falls as purchase multiples rise relative to what lenders will fund. Source: wss technicals career, wss credit distressed · Applied: TXU ~18% vs. EA ~65%

Accretion / dilution — Whether an acquisition raises or lowers the buyer's earnings per share. Compares the target's earnings yield with the after-tax cost of whatever pays for it (cash, debt or stock). Source: wss capital markets ma · Applied: Netflix/WBD all-cash switch

IPO pop — First-day price jump above the offer price. Good PR, but it is value transferred from the company to the investors allocated shares. Source: wss capital markets ma · Applied: Figma (~$3B left on the table)

Greenshoe (overallotment option) — Underwriters sell up to 15% more shares than the base deal and cover by buying in the market (supporting the price) or exercising the option (if it rises). Source: wss capital markets ma · Applied: SpaceX IPO

Rollover equity — Sellers reinvest part of their proceeds into the post-buyout company, cutting the cash needed and keeping founders aligned. Source: wss capital markets ma

Private credit / direct lending — Loans made directly by non-bank funds to companies, held to maturity rather than syndicated or traded. Floating-rate, usually senior secured, priced at a premium for illiquidity and speed. Source: wss credit distressed · Applied: EA buyout, First Brands, Lakers/Delaware Life

PIK (payment-in-kind) — Interest paid by adding to the loan balance instead of in cash. A borrower-stress signal when switched on mid-life. Source: wss credit distressed

BDC (business development company) / gating — Fund vehicles that hold private loans and offer periodic liquidity, typically capped ~5% of NAV per quarter. Gating is enforcing the cap when redemption requests exceed it. Source: wss credit distressed, wss private markets wealth · Applied: BCRED, Blue Owl

Liability management exercise (LME) — Out-of-court maneuvers that let some creditors jump the queue: uptiers, drop-downs of assets into new subsidiaries, guarantee releases. Creditor-on-creditor conflict. Source: wss credit distressed · Applied: Caesars · Argues with: canon jensen meckling agency theory (the debt side of agency costs)

Recovery rate — Cents on the dollar lenders get back after default. First-lien recoveries have fallen from ~80 to ~60 as loan-only structures removed junior cushions. Source: wss credit distressed

Credit default swap (CDS) — Insurance on a borrower's default. The spread divided by loss-given-default approximates annual default probability. Source: wss credit distressed, wss ai economics · Applied: Oracle as the "anti-AI trade"

Duration / DV01 — Duration: a bond's price sensitivity to yield, in years. DV01: dollar change in value for a one-basis-point move. The unit macro traders size risk in. Source: wss rates macro, wss trading hedge funds

Convexity — Duration changes as yields move; positive convexity means gains on falling yields exceed losses on rising ones. Mortgages are negatively convex because borrowers refinance. Source: wss rates macro

Yield curve / steepener — Yields across maturities. A steepener profits when long rates rise relative to short rates. Source: wss rates macro

QE vs. reserve management vs. Treasury buybacks — QE: the Fed buys long bonds to push down long rates. Reserve management: buying bills to keep bank reserves ample, not a policy signal. Treasury buybacks: the Treasury retiring old bonds, whose effect depends on how they are funded. Source: wss rates macro

CPI vs. PCE — Two inflation measures. The Fed targets PCE (broader, reweights as people substitute); CPI weighs housing more heavily and runs higher. Source: wss rates macro

SOFR — The overnight secured rate on Treasury-backed repo; the benchmark that replaced LIBOR for floating-rate loans and swaps. Source: wss rates macro

Basis trade — Long cash Treasuries, short Treasury futures, funded in repo, capturing a small price gap with high leverage. Blows up when repo funding or margins tighten. Source: wss trading hedge funds

Pod shop (multi-manager hedge fund) — Many small teams with tight stop-losses and central risk control (Citadel, Millennium). Pass-through fees let the platform charge for costs. Source: wss trading hedge funds

Sharpe ratio — Excess return divided by volatility; return per unit of risk. Source: wss trading hedge funds · Argues with: quant-backtesting/ on overfit Sharpe

Put/call ratio — Volume of puts relative to calls; extreme lows read as complacency. Source: wss trading hedge funds

TVPI / DPI — Total value to paid-in (marks plus cash returned) vs. distributions to paid-in (cash actually returned). DPI is the one that pays LPs. Source: wss private markets wealth

Secondaries / continuation fund — LP-led: an investor sells its fund stake. GP-led: the manager moves assets it still likes into a new vehicle, giving old LPs an exit. Source: wss private markets wealth

Denominator effect — When public stocks fall faster than private marks, private assets become overweight, forcing institutions to pause commitments or sell. Source: wss private markets wealth · Applied: Yale's ~$6bn sale

Evergreen / semi-liquid fund — Open-ended private-markets fund sold to individuals with periodic, capped redemptions. Carry is often charged annually on unrealized gains. Source: wss private markets wealth

Project finance / SPV — Funding one asset in a separate entity whose debt is repaid by that asset's cash flows, keeping it off the sponsor's balance sheet. Source: wss ai economics, wss private markets wealth · Applied: Meta Hyperion, xAI

Vendor financing / backstop — A supplier guaranteeing or funding its customers' purchases. Grows sales; couples supplier and customer risk. Source: wss ai economics · Applied: NVIDIA and OpenAI data centers

Useful-life debate (AI chips) — Depreciating GPUs over 5–6 years instead of 2–3 flatters earnings if the chips are obsolete sooner. Source: wss ai economics · Applied: Burry vs. Meta/Oracle

ETF creation / redemption — Authorized participants swap baskets of the underlying securities for ETF shares (and back) in kind. This arbitrage keeps the price near NAV and lets the fund shed low-basis stock without realizing gains, which is the source of the ETF tax advantage. Source: wss trading hedge funds

Cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) — Treasury futures can be settled with any bond from an eligible basket; the short delivers whichever is cheapest after the conversion factor. Futures DV01 ≈ CTD DV01 ÷ conversion factor. Source: wss rates macro, wss trading hedge funds

Carry trade — Borrowing in a low-yielding currency or rate and investing in a higher-yielding one, earning the spread until the funding currency jumps. The yen carry unwind of 2024 is the channel's case. Source: wss rates macro

Unitranche — A single blended loan from a direct lender replacing separate senior and junior tranches; one document, one lender group, leverage up to ~7x in the channel's examples. Source: wss credit distressed

Capital solutions — Bespoke financing for companies that are stressed or unusual rather than bankrupt (e.g. lending against a law firm's case book). Where distressed-debt capital went during a decade with few defaults. Source: wss credit distressed

Direct listing — Going public by listing existing shares without an underwritten offering or bookbuild; no IPO discount, but no new money (unless a primary direct listing) and no greenshoe price support. Source: wss capital markets ma · Applied: Spotify

Block trade — A large sale of existing shares (typically 1–10% of a company) placed overnight by a bank at a discount, often bought by the bank at risk. Source: wss capital markets ma

Liquidation preference — Venture preferred stock's right to get its money back before common in a sale. Later rounds often rank senior, so in a sale below the last valuation early investors act like a junior tranche. Source: wss private markets wealth, apply wss to venture

Continuation vehicle — A new fund a GP creates to buy assets from its own older fund, priced by secondary buyers, so existing LPs can sell or roll. ~$70bn of the $160bn 2024 secondaries market was GP-led. Source: wss private markets wealth · Contrast: opportunity funds such as Primary Select add capital instead (primary venture partners insights)

Cross-cluster argument spines (where the books fight)

These are the most valuable threads in the program — follow them to see how frameworks contradict, refine, and build on each other. Each spine is a path through the canon.

  1. What is a moat? Porter (forces) → Christensen (disruption) → Grove (inflection) → Helmer (7 powers) → Thiel (monopoly)
  2. How to decide under uncertainty: Kahneman (biases) → Munger (inversion) → Tetlock (calibrate) → Mauboussin (skill vs luck) → Bezos (70% + reversibility)
  3. How organizations actually decide: Kahneman (System 1/2) ↔ Klein (trust intuition) → Kahneman-Noise (reduce scatter) → March (garbage can) → Allison (rational/process/politics)
  4. Persuasion — two schools: Fisher/Ury (rational, interests-based) ↔ Voss (emotional, empathy-based); Cialdini (the levers) → Carnegie (sincerity) ↔ Greene/Pfeffer (raw power)
  5. Changing people and orgs: Schein (diagnosis) → Kotter (top-down 8 steps) ↔ Heath/Switch (bottom-up Rider/Elephant/Path) → Horowitz (culture = action) → Clear (habit systems)
  6. Find the one thing: Rumelt (kernel) → Rumelt (crux) → Goldratt (constraint) → Meadows (leverage point) — Martin: refuse the false tradeoff
  7. Execution chain: Rumelt → Bungay (intent) → Marquet (authority) → Larson (load) → Bossidy/Charan → 4DX (protect from whirlwind)
  8. Surviving the tails: Taleb-Black Swan → Taleb-Antifragile → Klarman (margin of safety) → Ries (small capped bets)
  9. Why moats exist (rigorous): Mankiw (markets) → Akerlof (asymmetry/signaling) → Helmer (switching/network) → Shapiro/Varian (lock-in) → Parker/Cusumano/Hagiu (platforms)
  10. The personal OS: Covey (Q2) → Newport (deep work) → Clear (habit systems)
  11. Does public disclosure level the field? sec-filing-intelligence (mandatory disclosure ⇒ no asymmetry barrier) ↔ bloomberg-terminal-instrumentation (symmetric corpus, asymmetric clock) → Shannon (content vs. channel) → Klarman (a long horizon is what makes the latency gap survivable)
  12. What is the analyst's actual job? sec-filing-intelligence (Layer 1 is commodity, Layer 3 is the product) → Damodaran, from a live Terminal (take the raw data, refuse the computed cost of capital — "it's my job to estimate") → a working buy-side analyst (take the financials, rebuild the drivers, hold consensus at arm's length) → accept the facts, refuse the judgment, build your own — see trading-floor-mechanics §3c
